Yes. I think several additional aspects contribute to the quality of a security code review comment.

First, evidence and confidence are important. Reviewers should distinguish between a confirmed vulnerability, a likely problem, and a possibility that requires further investigation. When practical, a minimal reproduction, attack scenario, failing test, or reference to relevant documentation can strengthen the comment.

Second, exploitability and preconditions deserve explicit consideration. Two defects with identical technical behavior may have very different security significance depending on whether the affected input is attacker-controlled, whether authentication is required, and whether the vulnerable path is externally reachable.

Third, scope and context matter. A high-quality comment should consider the surrounding architecture, trust boundaries, existing mitigations, and whether the problem occurs elsewhere in similar code rather than treating the reviewed line entirely in isolation.

Fourth, verifiability is useful. When possible, the comment should make it clear how a developer or reviewer can verify that the proposed fix actually resolves the problem, for example through a regression test or a specific security property that should hold after the change.

Finally, clarity and proportionality are important. Security comments should be concise, technically precise, constructive, and proportional to the actual risk. Overstating severity or using vague security terminology can make security review less effective even when the underlying observation is correct.

column9:
Precision: names the specific issue (race condition, use-after-free, injection, missing auth check) rather than a vague "this looks risky."
Exact location: points to the specific line, variable, or code path responsible, not just "somewhere in this function."
Accuracy: the issue actually has to be present as described — a misidentification doesn't just fail to help, it wastes the author's time and erodes trust in the reviewer's future comments ("crying wolf").
Root cause vs. symptom: names the underlying cause (e.g., unsynchronized shared state) rather than a pattern that merely correlates with the real problem.
Scope clarity: makes clear whether this is a one-off instance or a pattern likely repeated elsewhere in the codebase.
column11:
Causal mechanism: explains how the problem actually happens (e.g., "increment is a read + write, and two threads' operations can interleave"), not just an assertion that it's wrong.
Preconditions: states when the issue triggers — under concurrency, adversarial input, a specific config, etc.
Technical correctness: the explanation itself has to be right. A confident but wrong explanation is arguably worse than none, since it actively misleads.
Calibrated confidence: signals how sure the reviewer is ("99% sure about this" vs. an unqualified claim), so the author knows how much to independently verify.
Tied to the actual code: references the real construct in the diff rather than a generic textbook description of the vulnerability class.
column13:
Concrete consequence: names an actual outcome — DoS, data exposure, privilege escalation, memory corruption — instead of a generic "this is insecure."
Threat-model framing: describes who could trigger it and how (e.g., "a byzantine proposer sending malformed input"), so the reader sees a realistic attack path, not an abstract risk.
Proportionate severity: conveys how bad it is without over- or under-selling — exaggeration undermines trust just as much as understatement kills urgency.
Context sensitivity: accounts for whether the affected path is externally reachable, internal-only, or trusted-input, since that changes how much the impact actually matters here.
column15:
Actionability: a concrete next step — a code change, the right primitive to use (Interlocked.Increment), or at least the correct general pattern.
Correctness and completeness: the fix has to close the whole issue, not just the visible half (checking a return value and freeing the associated resource).
Fit with existing conventions: a technically valid fix that ignores the codebase's idioms or constraints is lower quality even when "correct."
Room for reviewer judgment: for architecture-level issues, pointing at the right category of fix ("use a vetted crypto library") can be as valuable as literal code, and is sometimes more appropriate than dictating an exact patch.
column16:
Tone and framing: whether the comment reads as collaborative ("this needs to be X because Y") or dismissive/condescending. A technically excellent comment that's abrasive gets argued with or ignored rather than fixed.
Calibrated confidence: distinct from Reason's correctness — whether the reviewer flags their own uncertainty so the author knows how much independent verification is warranted. This showed up explicitly in the OpenTelemetry example ("99% sure") and is a real quality signal that doesn't map cleanly onto any of the four dimensions.
Signal-to-noise: a comment can score well on all four dimensions and still bury the point in hedging or tangents. Saying it concisely is itself a quality marker.
Severity/priority signaling: whether the comment communicates how blocking the issue is ("must fix before merge" vs. "worth a follow-up"), which matters for triage when a PR has many competing comments.
Verifiability: whether the author (or another reviewer) can independently confirm the claim — a repro step, a CWE/CVE reference, a doc link — rather than having to trust the reviewer's authority outright.
Generalizability: whether the comment helps the author recognize the broader pattern so they avoid the mistake elsewhere, not just patch this one instance.
column17:
The four dimensions map closely onto a well-written vulnerability disclosure (what/where, root cause, severity, remediation) — a good sign the framework is capturing the right underlying structure of technical security communication, not an arbitrary taxonomy.
They aren't fully independent. Identification functions as a gatekeeper: without it, Reason/Impact/Solution have nothing to attach to. It might be worth scoring Identification as a precondition rather than a peer dimension — e.g., a comment can't score above some ceiling on the other three if Identification is wrong or missing.
Relative importance likely shifts with audience expertise and issue novelty: a well-known bug class ("classic TOCTOU") may need less spelled-out Reason/Solution for an experienced security team, while the same comment aimed at a broad open-source contributor base benefits from all four being explicit, since you can't assume a shared baseline.

Whether it explains the condition under which the issue can happen.
Whether the comment is specific enough that the developer can understand the concern without having to ask for more clarification.

For example, saying "possible panic" is useful, but saying that msg.Hashes[0] can panic when the list is empty is much more useful.
column11:
Reason is important because it helps the developer understand why the code is unsafe instead of just telling them that something is wrong. This is also useful in preventing the same type of issue from being introduced somewhere else.

I would evaluate Reason based on:

Whether the comment explains the technical cause of the problem.
Whether it connects the code behavior to the security concern.
Whether the explanation is technically correct and relevant.
Whether it gives enough context for the developer to understand why the current implementation is unsafe.

The explanation does not always need to be long. Even one or two sentences can be enough as long as they explain the actual cause.
column13:
Impact helps communicate how serious the issue could become if it is not fixed. There is a big difference between something that may cause a small reliability issue and something that allows an attacker to crash a service or expose credentials.

I would evaluate Impact based on:

Whether the comment explains what could happen if the issue is exploited.
Whether it identifies who or what could be affected.
Whether it describes the security consequence, such as data exposure, DoS, privilege escalation, or unauthorized access.
Whether the stated impact is realistic and supported by the code instead of being exaggerated.

Mentioning the attacker or triggering scenario is also useful when it is relevant. For example, explaining that malformed input from an untrusted peer could crash the service gives much more context than simply saying that a panic is possible.
column15:
A security review comment becomes more useful when it gives the developer a clear direction for fixing the issue. It does not necessarily need to provide the complete implementation, but it should ideally give enough information to move toward the correct solution.

I would evaluate Solution based on:

Whether the suggested fix actually addresses the root cause.
Whether the recommendation is specific and actionable.
Whether it follows the language or project's normal coding practices.
Whether it avoids introducing another security or reliability issue.
Whether the reviewer provides an example or alternative approach when the correct fix may not be obvious.

I would not require every review comment to include exact replacement code. Sometimes the reviewer may identify the issue correctly but not have enough context to decide the best implementation. In those cases, giving the expected secure behavior is still useful.
column16:
Yes. I think there are a few other aspects that affect the quality of a security code review comment.

One is accuracy/confidence. A comment should distinguish between a confirmed vulnerability and something the reviewer thinks may be risky. Otherwise developers may spend time investigating issues that are not actually possible.

Another is severity or priority. It is useful to communicate whether something is a critical security concern that should block the change or more of a defense-in-depth improvement.

I would also consider clarity and tone. Security comments should be direct, but they should focus on the code and the risk rather than blaming the person who wrote it. This makes it easier to discuss the issue and get it fixed.

Finally, context is important. If exploitation depends on the input being attacker-controlled, a certain configuration being enabled, or another condition being true, mentioning that condition makes the comment much more useful.

For example, a short comment with very strong Identification and Impact may still be useful even without a detailed Solution. column9: Criteria I'd use: (1) Does it name the exact expression or symbol, not just the file or the general area? Example 2 says "possible panic" but never names msg.Hashes[0], so the author has to rediscover the bug themselves. (2) Does it state the triggering precondition? A security issue is a claim about reachable state, so identification is incomplete without the condition that reaches it, e.g. when a peer sends an empty Hashes slice.(3) Is the claim falsifiable? If a comment is vague enough that it cannot be shown wrong, it cannot be checked either, and it will be dismissed. (4) Does it distinguish the symptom from the defect? "Panic" is the symptom; the defect is indexing attacker-controlled data without a length check. Comments that stop at the symptom tend to get symptom-level fixes. (5) Does it say whether this is a single instance or a pattern repeated elsewhere in the diff? (6) Does it use a recognizable category name (improper access control, log injection, TOCTOU) so the thread is greppable later and connects to existing knowledge?
column11: Criteria: (1) Mechanism versus restatement. "++ does a read and a write and they are not atomic together" is a mechanism. "This is racy" is just re-asserting the conclusion. (2) Does it name the violated invariant rather than only the language feature? The OpenTelemetry comment is strong because it explains that the lock is keyed by tag value and therefore does not serialize a shared counter. That generalizes; "use Interlocked" does not. (3) Does it surface its assumptions about the threat model, caller, or concurrency, so someone with more context can rebut it? An unrebuttable reason is not a reason. (4) Is it independently verifiable by the author, ideally by writing a test or reading a spec rather than trusting the reviewer? (5) Calibration. I read "99% sure about this" in the Telegraf example as a quality signal, not a weakness. Reviewers who state confidence let authors allocate verification effort correctly. (6) Does it separate "this is wrong" from "this is not obviously right"? Both are legitimate review outcomes and conflating them wastes time.
column13: Criteria: (1) Is the attacker model stated? Who has to do what, and what access do they need beforehand? The Cosmos comment works because it names the actor (byzantine proposer), the input (malformed txs), and the outcome (node crash, DoS). (2) Is severity proportionate to reachability? Inflated impact is the single most damaging failure mode in security review. Once a reviewer has called two things "RCE" that were not, their real findings get ignored, so overstatement has a cost that persists past the current PR. I would rate an accurate "low severity, still worth fixing" above an inflated one. (3) Is the consequence expressed as a security property that breaks (availability, confidentiality, integrity, trust boundary crossed) rather than a generic "this is dangerous"? (4) Blast radius: self-inflicted versus remotely triggerable, one user versus all users, recoverable versus not. (5) Does it admit when impact is unknown instead of guessing? "I cannot tell if this input is attacker-reachable, but if it is, this is a crash" is more useful than a confident wrong number.
column15: I rate this lower than the other three deliberately. Identification, Reason, and Impact are things the code author usually cannot supply for themselves, which is the entire reason review exists. A solution often can be, because the author knows the codebase better than the reviewer does. A wrong or partial suggested fix is actively negative: it gets applied verbatim, the thread is marked resolved, and the vulnerability survives with a security review comment sitting on top of it saying it was handled. Criteria: (1) Correctness before completeness. (2) Does it address the root cause and every instance of the class in the diff, or just the one line? (3) Does it state the property the fix must preserve, so the author can choose a different implementation? That is more durable than a code snippet. (4) Does it acknowledge tradeoffs (performance, API compatibility, error-path behavior) instead of implying the fix is free? (5) Does it include a way to verify? Almost no review comments I have seen say "and add a regression test that feeds an empty slice here," which is why the same bug class comes back. (6) Framing. The Telegraf "so how about:" phrasing gets adopted more often than a mandate, and adoption is part of whether the comment was actually good.
column16: Four things IRIS does not capture. (1) Evidence. All four attributes are assertions. None covers how the reviewer knows: a failing test, a PoC input, a spec or CWE reference, a static analysis trace, a link to a past incident. Evidence is what converts a disputed comment into a fixed bug, and it is separable from Reason, since a correct explanation can still be unsupported. (2) Calibration. Explicit confidence, and explicit uncertainty about reachability. A comment that says "I could not confirm this path is attacker-reachable" is higher quality than one that omits the doubt, but IRIS would score them identically or penalize the honest one. (3) Priority signalling. Whether the reviewer considers this merge-blocking or a nit. Security comments that arrive undifferentiated from style comments get batched and deferred. (4) Scope. Whether the comment tells the author this pattern likely appears elsewhere and the rest of the file or module should be audited. Single-site fixes for class bugs are extremely common.
column17:
One methodological note, offered in case you are building a scoring rubric or an automated judge from these attributes. The four attributes are unlikely to be independent or compensatory. Identification is a gate: a comment with no identifiable defect cannot be rescued by an excellent Solution, and Reason is partly entangled with Identification since the mechanism often is the precise location. If the rubric sums or averages IRIS scores, it will rank a vague-but-verbose comment above a terse-but-precise one, which inverts what practitioners actually value. I would test whether a gated or lexicographic scoring behaves better than an additive one, and I would check inter-rater reliability per attribute separately rather than on the aggregate, since I expect Impact to have much lower agreement than Identification.

Second, quality here is audience-relative in a way the framing does not address. The PR author needs Identification, Reason, and Solution. A security auditor reading the review history months later needs Identification, Reason, and Impact, and does not care about Solution at all. Worth deciding which reader the construct is defined for.

Third, if you have access to the outcome data, it would strengthen the work considerably to check whether IRIS attributes predict whether the comment was actually resolved with a committed fix, rather than only whether practitioners say the attributes feel important. Self-reported importance and behavioural effect diverge a lot in code review.

column9:
Criteria for evaluating Identification in an SCRC

I would evaluate Identification based on whether the review comment precisely identifies the security issue, the specific code element involved, and the conditions under which the vulnerability can occur. A high-quality SCRC should clearly distinguish the affected code from surrounding context and provide enough technical detail for the developer to locate and understand the issue without ambiguity. I would also consider the accuracy, specificity, reproducibility, and clarity of the identification, as well as whether it enables the developer to verify the reported security concern independently.
column11: When evaluating “Reason,” I would assess whether the comment technically and clearly explains the mechanism underlying the security issue or the causal relationship behind it. I would consider it important that the explanation connects the affected code to the resulting security impact and provides sufficient technical detail for the developer to understand why the code is problematic. The explanation should be accurate, relevant, verifiable, and proportionate to the complexity of the issue; a longer explanation alone does not indicate higher quality.
column13: When evaluating “Impact,” I would assess whether the comment accurately and technically justifiably describes the potential consequences of the identified security issue. I would consider it important that the comment connects the vulnerability to the specific security impact, such as denial of service, unauthorized access, data leakage, data loss, or system crash, where these consequences are reasonably supported by the code and the execution environment. I would also evaluate the accuracy, relevance, appropriate assessment of severity, and verifiability of the stated impact. I would not consider a comment to be of high quality if it attributes exaggerated or unsubstantiated security consequences to the issue
column15: When evaluating Solution, I would assess whether the comment provides specific, technically correct, and actionable guidance for addressing the identified security issue. I would consider it important that the proposed solution directly addresses the identified problem, is clear, and describes the necessary changes in a way that the developer can effectively implement. When the nature of the issue allows for a specific code-level fix, providing concrete corrective code or an equivalent, precise implementation-level recommendation should significantly strengthen the quality of the SCRC. I would also evaluate the technical correctness, feasibility, security implications, and whether the proposed fix could introduce new problems or security risks.
column16: Yes. In addition to identification, reason, impact, and solution, I would consider context, adequate supporting evidence, clarity, and proportionality to be important characteristics. A high-quality SCRC should take into account the context of the system and execution environment, so that the finding is not only theoretically correct but also relevant to the specific environment. It is also important for the comment to distinguish demonstrated issues from assumptions and to be supported by appropriate evidence or reproducible behavior. The wording should be clear, objective, and proportionate to the severity of the issue.
column17: I believe that one of the most important characteristics of a high-quality security code review is that the comment should not only identify the problem, but also help the developer understand, verify, and appropriately address it. I consider technical accuracy, consideration of the relevant context, and ensuring that findings are supported by evidence and reproducible behavior to be particularly important. I also consider it important to assess whether the code may contain potentially malicious or intentionally hidden functionality, such as a backdoor, conditionally activated malicious code, or a component inserted as part of a cyberattack. Such code may only become active under specific circumstances, for example after being deployed or integrated into a particular system. However, I consider it important that such findings are based on appropriate technical evidence rather than assumptions.

My criteria: minimal suggestion fitting existing style, explains why the fix closes the issue rather than patching the symptom, mentions alternatives when several exist, includes a short code sketch for non-obvious cases. Directional guidance is often worth more than fully prescribed implementation.

IRIS covers the informational core well. Three additions: 
1. Correctness/validity - a false-positive security comment burns trust and trains authors to ignore reviews, so accuracy is the precondition for all four attributes. 
2. Clarity and tone - concise, respectful phrasing security findings can read as accusations and derail collaboration. 
3. Verifiability - how to reproduce the issue or a suggested test proving the fix, plus references like CWE or OWASP entries which strengthen credibility and teach beyond this one change.

Therefore, I value a reason more for being clear, technically grounded, and open to verification than for appearing definitive.

I would evaluate whether the described impact is a plausible consequence of the identified issue, whether the causal connection is clear, and whether the severity of the consequence is presented proportionally. Since impact often describes a hypothetical scenario rather than an observed outcome, I also think it is important to distinguish plausible risks from speculative or exaggerated ones.

I consider impact useful for understanding the significance and priority of an issue, but somewhat secondary to correctly identifying and explaining the issue itself. A review comment can still be technically useful even if it does not fully describe the possible consequences.
column15:
I would evaluate a proposed solution based on whether it is technically correct, actionable, feasible within the project context, and actually addresses the identified issue without introducing unnecessary changes or new problems.

However, I do not consider providing a solution to be an obligation of the reviewer. A reviewer may identify a valid problem without knowing the best implementation-level fix, especially when the contributor has more context about the code being changed. In that sense, a concrete solution is valuable additional guidance, but I would not treat its absence as making an otherwise accurate and useful review comment low quality. The contributor should ultimately remain responsible for deciding how to address the issue in the submitted code.

column9: There are no fixed formal criteria for SCRC identification. In practice, we primarily use Claude Code for code review. Key indicators include whether the comment focuses on security risks, locates specific code issues, addresses root security causes, and provides actionable fixes. Human verification is still needed to filter AI false positives.
column11: There are no fixed formal criteria for evaluating the Reason of a SCRC. A typical example is multi‑threaded loops, where actual execution order differs from written code order, such as execution sequence in NodeJS asynchronous code blocks. Key indicators include whether the reason accurately explains the underlying logic behind the security risk, correctly reflects runtime behaviour, matches the observed vulnerability, and clearly illustrates why the issue introduces security exposure.

column9: The comment should clearly state the reproduction steps of the vulnerability, mark the exact line‑number of problematic code, and explicitly describe what security flaw exists.
column11:
The reason part should explain the root‑cause of the vulnerability, and clarify which code modules may be affected after applying the fix.
A high‑quality reason explanation should uncover the fundamental root cause behind the vulnerability, rather than only describing the surface‑level phenomenon.
It needs to clarify which part of server‑side logic is defective, such as weak authentication, insufficient session binding or loose behaviour verification.
In addition, the comment should mention which modules or functions may be impacted after applying a security fix, so developers can anticipate potential side‑effects.
column13:
The impact description should clarify what resources could be abused, the severity level of risk, and the potential losses caused by the vulnerability.
Developers can determine the priority of bug fixes according to its consequences.
column15:
A qualified solution should provide at least one concrete, actionable fix.
It should specify the exact changes for target code lines, rather than vague suggestions.
The reviewer also needs to consider whether this modification would introduce new security‑related risks.
